key.explanation: Collection should be limited to a stated purpose, protection built in by default rather than on request, and a third-party processor's compliance verified before data reaches it. Collecting now for a feature that may never exist fails the first of those.

The method sorts necessity, and it only works if the categories are used: naming what will not be done is what makes the ordering real. A regulatory mandate is a constraint on the release rather than a candidate within it.

The mainstream buyer needs a complete offer: the product plus references, reliability and support. Concentrating on one narrow segment is what makes that complete offer achievable and the references credible.

One purchase can stack a functional need, an emotional one and a social one at once, and the commuter names all three without using the words. Naming the product, the frequency or the price answers a different question.

Definition is what the product does and is largely internal, for the team and its partners to build against. Positioning is how it changes things for the user and why they should care. One sentence cannot be both.

Functional requirements say what the system does; quality requirements — performance, security, availability — say how well and under what conditions. The 30-second bound and the role restriction constrain the export the first statement introduces.

Cost-based pricing is the fallback for when the deployment and the customer's economics are unknown. Here both are known and quantified, so the price should be set against the ₹2.4 crore of value created.

Value has to be communicated in the order the buyer moves through: make the problem and the relevant value understandable first, then introduce alternatives and proof as the decision approaches. Arriving with proof first is arriving too early.
Pricing serves a business objective — profitability, share, market saturation, segment entry or defence — and the objective decides the price rather than the other way round.
A go to market strategy decides how a product reaches and converts its users, and a software product's route can lean on free access and virality in a way a physical product's cannot.
A product family is a set of diverse but connected products under one strong brand, held together by consistent branding, the trust it carries and cross-selling.
A service strategy names the services that complete the whole product — professional services such as implementation and consulting, and product services such as support and training.

The heartbeat principle fixes a predictable release rhythm and plans backwards from it; upward compatibility keeps version N's behaviour working in N+1; and a change control board decides what enters a release.

The product manager owns what is built and why — vision, roadmap, pricing, market, business model, facing outward — while the product owner owns how the team builds it, through backlog, stories and sprint priorities.

Problem-solution fit proves a real problem and a valued solution for early users at MVP stage on qualitative learning; product-market fit proves scalable, repeated demand in a large market on quantitative traction.
Embedded software controls a machine, running on limited resources under specific device conditions, so its job is to make a physical device work rather than to be the value.

The business model canvas sets a value proposition against customer segments, channels and relationships on one side and key activities, resources, partners and cost against revenue streams on the other.

A startup is a temporary organisation experimenting toward a business model under uncertainty, and bootstrapped, funded and corporate ventures each trade a different resource against a different constraint.
The value proposition canvas maps a customer profile of jobs, pains and gains onto a value map of products, pain relievers and gain creators.

Product thinking judges a product on five dimensions at once — value to the customer, scalability, sustainability, responsibility, and profitability or impact — and the work is managing the trade-offs between them.

The Kano model sorts features into must-be, performance, delighter and indifferent, and cost-value prioritisation ranks them quantitatively — with time as a third axis, because a delayed feature changes category.
A product family is a set of diverse but connected products under one strong brand, held together by consistent branding, the trust it carries and cross-selling.
A startup usually has no history to extrapolate, so it forecasts from market size and analogues and then updates the estimate as real data arrives — the habit superforecasting describes.
A published price can be read backwards as a diagnosis: what the firm believes its customers value, which segments it is serving, and where it thinks its advantage lies.
Where the beneficiary cannot pay, the product must still be built to scale — technology from day one, built only where it is needed, and an intermediary that absorbs the coordination.

Validation asks whether a solution works for real users: build a core product in the least time and cost, test it for repeatable use, and treat validated learning as data rather than praise, ending in problem-solution fit.
A company vision describes the future of the whole firm and endures; a product vision says why one product exists and evolves with it.

A launch is planned rather than announced: assess the internal and external context, set objectives, choose the customers, then settle positioning against competitors, obstacles, segments and advantages.
Tailorability is how far one product can be fitted to many customers, and configuration — setting parameters within what the product already supports — is its cheapest form.
A learning loop runs build, measure, learn on a small experiment so market risk falls and product-market fit arrives sooner than a full build would allow.
The four growth strategies are sales-led, marketing-led, product-led and ecosystem-led, and each rests on a different asset: relationships, brand, the product experience, or the partner network.
Product planning decides what to build, when, why and for whom, and its three approaches are requirements-driven planning, data-driven planning and market-driven planning.
A requirement moves through eight states in the repository — new, approved, specified, selected and onward to released — driven by elicitation, triage, analysis, selection, build and validation.
The three software delivery models are on-premise, SaaS and managed services, and they differ in who owns the infrastructure, who operates it, and how much tailoring the customer can do.
Vanity metrics are numbers that feel good without changing a decision; actionable metrics are those a team can act on and extrapolate to a segment and a market.
A roadmap translates strategy into a sequence of releases on a time axis. Deferral is part of that decision, which is why an inventory of eventual contents is a different artefact.

₹1,800 a year against ₹5,400 is a three-year payback, and four years of retention gives about ₹7,200 of lifetime gross profit. Both facts are true at once, and the second does not remove the cash risk the first creates.

Desirability and feasibility both hold; viability fails, because ₹400 of revenue against ₹430 of cost means every additional driver loses money and the case states the cost does not fall with scale. All three checks have to clear.

Total is everyone the product could in principle serve, 900,000. Certification is a real constraint that narrows it to 90,000 serviceable. The obtainable figure is bounded by both competition and the firm's own reach, which is why 4,000 is the number a plan should be built on.

Customer requirements are business needs and aspirations; the product requirement is what the product will do about them; project requirements break that down for a release. Standardising is what turns one hospital's need into something many can buy.
The canvas exists to make assumptions explicit and cheap to change. Holding it stable to look consistent is the one use that removes its value.

Competition is whatever the customer would otherwise do about this job - here a spreadsheet, a person, and doing nothing at all, which between them cover thirty-five of the forty teams. Adjacent software serving a different need is not an alternative.

Registrations, page views and press mentions accumulate and cannot fall, so they cannot tell progress from activity. Flat weekly active use is the figure that would answer whether the product works, and a number with no owner and no threshold cannot trigger anything.
Problem, solution, key metrics, and unfair advantage are the Lean Canvas additions. Customer segments, channels, cost structure, and revenue structure carry across from the Business Model Canvas.

The named failures are communicating too late, using the wrong channels, and sending a message that does not match the customer's need. Good products fizzle when the value is never articulated, not when it is mispriced.

Customer requirements arrive as business needs and aspirations. Standardising generalises one customer's need so the product serves many; project requirements are the internal breakdown engineering owns for a release.
Vision comes first, and the other two translate it. Definition is what the product does, written for the team and its partners; positioning is how it impacts users and why they should use it.
The evolution is deliberate ordering, not accident: the team launched on iPhone knowing many users were on Android. A roadmap is a smart sequence for developing, releasing, and evolving a solution.
Must have covers what the product cannot function without — booking, payments, GPS. Ratings are should have: valuable, and not load-bearing.
The unit follows the customer relationship model. SaaS acquires a customer who transacts repeatedly, so the account is the unit; a marketplace relationship is transactional, so the transaction is.
TAM measures the prize, SAM what you are permitted and able to reach, SOM what you can take given who already holds it. They are narrowing constraints, not a headline figure.
The four are beachhead focus, simplification, trust and reliability, and ecosystem fit. Mainstream customers avoid risk, so the work is lowering perceived risk rather than signalling through price.
This one purchase stacks a functional, an emotional, and a social need. Cost enters only through customer value, which is benefit minus cost — it is not one of the layers of the job.
MoSCoW is an acronym — must, should, could, won't — used as a filter rather than a ranking. Naming what won't be done is the half that makes scope control real.
A roadmap translates strategy into releases along a time axis, over a three-to-five-year horizon. WhatsApp's iPhone-first launch, with Android around 2011, is the lecture's worked sequence.
